Nestling Weka (Gallirallus australis) hatch from eggs incubated at 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C] after a developmental period of approximately 27 days [ab = approximately 27 days], a duration that reflects the thermoregulatory demands of embryonic growth within the calcareous egg. The newly emerged downy chick weighs just 52.25 grams [Ww0 = 52.25 grams] at first feeding, representing a modest initial wet mass that necessitates intensive parental provisioning to support rapid feather development and skeletal elongation. This initial mass is critical for survival, as the altricial nestling must quickly gain weight to reach the fledgling stage. Field observations of captive broods indicate that the time since birth at fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and nest departure, occurs at approximately 70 days [tx = approximately 70 days] under the same ambient temperature regime of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], though a range extending from 40 to 108 days has been reported in the literature depending on food availability and brood size. The period from hatching to fledging thus encompasses a substantial investment of parental energy, with the chick dependent on both parents for thermoregulation and food delivery during this extended nestling phase. Post-fledging, the juvenile bird must rapidly acquire foraging skills to reach nutritional independence.

Sexual maturation in the Weka follows a predictable schedule when birds are maintained at a stable body temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], with puberty estimated at 210 days since birth [tp = 210 days since birth]. This relatively early onset of gonadal activity is characteristic of many rallid species inhabiting temperate environments where seasonal resource pulses favor rapid reproductive maturation. The attainment of reproductive maturity is closely tied to the acquisition of adult body mass, as females require substantial energy reserves to initiate egg production. The ultimate wet weight for females reaches approximately 753 grams [Wwi = approximately 753 grams], whereas males, which are the larger sex in this species, attain an ultimate wet weight of roughly 1034 grams [Wwi = roughly 1034 grams]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism likely reflects differential selective pressures related to male-male competition for territories and female choice during the breeding season. The male's larger frame may also confer advantages in defending nest sites and provisioning the brooding female. In contrast to many other rails, the Weka exhibits a relatively rapid growth trajectory, achieving near-adult mass within the first year post-hatching under optimal conditions.

The first successful breeding event in Weka populations studied under controlled thermal conditions at 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C] occurs at approximately 474.5 days since birth [tR = approximately 474.5 days since birth], a timing that reflects social constraints on reproduction. This timing of first reproduction, occurring approximately sixteen months after hatching, is delayed relative to the attainment of puberty, suggesting that social factors, territory acquisition, and mate selection impose additional constraints on the initiation of reproductive activity. In high-density populations, younger individuals may be forced into subordinate breeding positions or deferred entirely from nesting during their first potential season. The interval between puberty and first reproduction thus represents a crucial life-history phase during which the immature bird must secure a breeding territory and form a pair bond. Field records from both North and South Islands of New Zealand indicate substantial inter-annual variation in this timing, with birds on islands lacking mammalian predators exhibiting earlier first breeding compared to those on the mainland where predation pressure from stoats and ferrets is intense.

Reproductive output in the Weka is characterized by females producing three eggs per clutch [N_R_i = three eggs per clutch] and up to four clutches annually [F_R_i = up to four clutches annually] when food resources are abundant at the reference temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], yielding a maximum annual output of 12 eggs. This high annual fecundity, unusual among New Zealand's endemic flightless birds, reflects the species' capacity to capitalize on irruptive food supplies such as heavy fruiting of native shrubs or increased invertebrate abundance following rainfall. The three-egg clutch size is relatively invariant across the species' range, although clutch frequency shows pronounced plasticity in response to local resource availability. Females on offshore islands with reduced predator pressure and abundant food have been documented producing the full complement of four clutches per year, whereas mainland populations experiencing higher predation rates or food scarcity often produce only one or two clutches annually. This reproductive flexibility likely contributes to the species' remarkable success in colonizing novel habitats and its resilience to environmental perturbation, including the impacts of introduced mammalian predators and habitat modification.

Resting metabolic measurements conducted on adult Weka under thermoneutral conditions at 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C] reveal a maximum basal metabolic rate of 329 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 329 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value consistent with the elevated metabolic demands of a flightless, ground-dwelling bird inhabiting cool temperate rainforests. This relatively high oxygen consumption rate, expressed per individual rather than per gram of body mass, reflects the substantial energetic costs of thermoregulation, locomotion, and digestion in a species that must maintain activity throughout the year without the option of seasonal migration. Comparative data from other rallids of similar body size suggest that the Weka's metabolic rate is toward the upper end of the family distribution, possibly linked to its omnivorous diet and the need to process a wide range of food items including invertebrates, fruits, seeds, and occasionally small vertebrates. The maximum recorded longevity in wild Weka populations, determined from long-term banding studies at a body temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], is approximately 15.3 years [am = approximately 15.3 years], though most individuals in the wild do not survive beyond five to eight years due to predation and disease. This lifespan, calculated as 5584.5 days, is notable for a bird of its size and reflects the relatively slow life-history pace imposed by the unpredictable resource environment of New Zealand's temperate forests.
